title: Evaluation of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in pregnant and breastfeeding women.
ehr_evidence: Via an online questionnaire, we have inquired about the safety experience of 2192 pregnant or breastfeeding women vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2
summary: A cross-sectional self-reported online questionnaire study of 2192 pregnant and breastfeeding women in Slovakia and the Czech Republic assessing SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine safety, adverse event incidence, pregnancy outcomes, and vaccine efficacy
key_findings: Breastfeeding women had higher adverse event incidence than pregnant women, with significant differences for fatigue (RR 1.230, 95% CI 1.051-1.444, P = 0.0098), headache (RR 1.822, 95% CI 1.379-2.418, P < 0.0001), myalgia (RR 1.633, 95% CI 1.269-2.110, P < 0.0001), chills (RR 2.027, P < 0.0001), subfebrile temperature ≤ 38°C (RR 1.697, 95% CI 1.240-2.335, P = 0.0007), arthralgia (RR 1.924, 95% CI 1.340-2.776, P = 0.0002), fever > 38°C (RR 6.410, 95% CI 2.890-14.30, P < 0.0001), and shivers (RR 2.204, 95% CI 1.264-3.863, P = 0.0049)
No pattern of serious adverse events emerged; SAE incidence was 0.3% (7 SAEs in 2165 respondents)
93.1% of pregnancies were carried to term, 5.6% late preterm, 0.9% moderate preterm, 0.3% very preterm, with one spontaneous abortion
Two infants (0.63%) had confirmed congenital defects among those delivered after pregnancy vaccination
Vaccine efficacy was 96.3% (3.7% confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections after any dose)
Menstrual cycle bleeding disorders occurred in 0.7% of breastfeeding women after the first dose and 0.5% after the second dose
captured_features: Adverse event incidence (first vs second dose)
Vaccine type (Pfizer, Moderna, AstraZeneca, Janssen, Sputnik)
pathologies_diseases: Adverse events (fatigue, headache, myalgia, chills, fever, arthralgia, shivers, injection-site reactions)
population: 2192 pregnant and breastfeeding women from Slovakia and the Czech Republic, mean age 32.6 years (range 20-47)
limitations: Convenience sample with voluntary participation and no inclusion/exclusion criteria
Self-reported data collected by respondents rather than trained personnel, with no ability to resolve discrepancies
P-values reported without correction for multiplicity (12 comparisons)
Data recorded before the Omicron variant era and for monovalent vaccines only
Small sample sizes in some dose-combination groups prevented meaningful statistical comparison
Potential selection bias from voluntary isolation among vaccinated pregnant/postpartum respondents
